newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY C.BANK HEAD TRIGGERED DISMISSALS - SPOKESMAN.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY C.BANK HEAD TRIGGERED DISMISSALS - SPOKESMAN.

text.p: Hungarian government spokesman Elemer Kiss said on Thursday a letter from National Bank of Hungary (NBH) President Gyorgy Suranyi to Prime Minister Gyula Horn had triggered the dismissal of two NBH vice presidents.

Kiss told reporters that Horn agreed to the resignation offers of Frigyes Harshegyi and Sandor Czirjak, who authorised a contract that could cost the bank millions of dollars, after receiving a letter from Suranyi on October 15.

Harshegyi and Czirjak will resign effective December 31 following disclosures that they had authorised a foreign exchange options deal which has forced the bank to create substantial risk reserves, which are estimated to cost in excess of 3 billion forints.

The disclosure came at a time when Hungary's political establishment was already reeling from a scandal over a consulting contract made by the state privatisation agency, which led to the dismissal of the minister in charge and the agency's directors.

Kiss quoted Suranyi as saying in the letter to Horn that action must be taken as an NBH report had found that the vice-presidents made technical mistakes in the option deal in 1992 and caused substantial loss to the bank.
"After a letter like that it was no wonder that the Prime Minister agreed with their intention to resign," Kiss said.
However, Suranyi said earlier this week that he had proposed to Horn that the prime minister not accept the resignations.
He said the vice presidents made a serious mistake but with other decisions they had made substantial contribution to strengthening the NBH's prestige in Hungary and abroad.
"I recommended him not to accept the resignation offers, or at least not with an effect which is so close," Suranyi said.
He also denied any link with the privatisation scandal but said Horn's decision to approve the resignations must have been influenced by the political atmosphere.
"A very deep and clear differentiation between this case and another case which occupies the public opinion must be made," Suranyi said earlier this week.
"I am convinced that the prime minister's decision was not unaffected by the mood and circumstances among which we live now," he added.
